In other words, an orthogonal projection matrix [MATH: P_S=A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T] is a matrix that transforms any vector of the vector space into its projection to subspace [MATH: S] spanned by the columns of [MATH: A].

As we know, if [MATH: A] is the matrix whose columns are the linearly independent vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n] then the projection of a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto [MATH: S=\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}] is given by
[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = {\color{blue}A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T}\,\mathbf{x}.]
Now, if we denote [MATH: P_S = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T], then
[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = {\color{blue}P_S}\,\mathbf{x}.]
The matrix [MATH: P_S] is called the orthogonal projection matrix. In other words, an orthogonal projection matrix
[MATH: P_S=A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T]
is a matrix that transforms any vector of the vector space into its projection to subspace [MATH: S] spanned by the columns of [MATH: A].

Content:
Knowing this, we can define the orthogonal projection transformation [MATH: \mathbf{P}_{\!S}] as
[MATH: \mathbf{P}_{\!S}:	\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n]
such that
[MATH: \mathbf{x} \,\,\, \mapsto \textrm{proj}_S\,\mathbf{x}.]
It maps each vector from [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] into its orthogonal projection on [MATH: S].

Content:
Note: The matrix [MATH: P_S] is the standard matrix of the orthogonal projection transformation, that is, the matrix relative to the standard basis of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n.]

Therefore, [MATH: A] is an orthogonal projection matrix.

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that [MATH: Q] is an orthogonal projection matrix if and only if [MATH: Q^2=Q] and [MATH: Q^T=Q.]

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

  • [MATH: A] is not an orthogonal projection matrix. We have [MATH: A^T = A] but [MATH: A^{2}|= A ⋅ A; = [2|1; 1|3][2|1; 1|3]; = [5|5; 5|10]; ≠ A.]

  • [MATH: B] is not an orthogonal projection matrix. We have [MATH: B^{T} ≠ B.]

  • [MATH: C] is an orthogonal projection matrix. Indeed, [MATH: C^T = C] and [MATH: C^{2}|= C ⋅ C; = [(4)/(5)|(2)/(5); (2)/(5)|(1)/(5)][(4)/(5)|(2)/(5); (2)/(5)|(1)/(5)]; = (1)/(5)[4|2; 2|1] ⋅ (1)/(5)[4|2; 2|1]; = (1)/(25)[4|2; 2|1][4|2; 2|1]; = (1)/(25)[20|10; 10|5]; = [(4)/(5)|(2)/(5); (2)/(5)|(1)/(5)]; = C.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: C] only."

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
As we know, if [MATH: A] is the matrix whose columns are the linearly independent vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n] then the projection of a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto [MATH: S=\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}] is given by
[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = {\color{blue}A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T}\,\mathbf{x}.]
Now, if we denote [MATH: P_S = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T], then
[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = {\color{blue}P_S}\,\mathbf{x}.]
The matrix [MATH: P_S] is called the orthogonal projection matrix. In other words, an orthogonal projection matrix
[MATH: P_S=A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T]
is a matrix that transforms any vector of the vector space into its projection to subspace [MATH: S] spanned by the columns of [MATH: A].

Content:
Knowing this, we can define the orthogonal projection transformation [MATH: \mathbf{P}_{\!S}] as
[MATH: \mathbf{P}_{\!S}:	\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n]
such that
[MATH: \mathbf{x} \,\,\, \mapsto \textrm{proj}_S\,\mathbf{x}.]
It maps each vector from [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] into its orthogonal projection on [MATH: S].

Content:
Note: The matrix [MATH: P_S] is the standard matrix of the orthogonal projection transformation, that is, the matrix relative to the standard basis of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding a Matrix that Defines an Orthogonal Projection Onto the Subspace Spanned by a Vector

Example Prompt:
Find a matrix that defines the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^3] onto the subspace spanned by [MATH: [1; 2; − 3]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the matrix [MATH: P_S = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T] maps any vector [MATH: \mathbf x\in \mathbb{R}^n] onto its orthogonal projection in the subspace [MATH: S] spanned by the columns of the matrix [MATH: A.]

In our case, [MATH: [1; 2; − 3]] Therefore,
[MATH: P_{S}|= A(A^{T}A)^{− 1}A^{T}; = [1; 2; − 3]([1|2|− 3][1; 2; − 3])^{− 1}[1|2|− 3]; = [1; 2; − 3] ⋅ (14)^{− 1}[1|2|− 2]; = (1)/(14)[1; 2; − 3][1|2|− 3]; = (1)/(14)[1|2|− 3; 2|4|− 6; − 3|− 6|9].]

---

Item 5 — Example: Finding a Matrix That Defines an Orthogonal Projection Onto the Subspace Spanned by a Plane

Find a matrix that defines the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^3] onto the plane whose parametric equation is [MATH: \mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{v} + t\mathbf{w}], where
[MATH: [1; 2; 1]]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the matrix [MATH: P_S = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T] maps any vector [MATH: \mathbf x\in \mathbb{R}^n] onto its orthogonal projection in the subspace [MATH: S] spanned by the columns of the matrix [MATH: A.]

Notice that the plane [MATH: \mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{v}+t\mathbf{w}] is actually the subspace [MATH: \text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}\}.]
Hence, we have
[MATH: [1|1; 2|− 1; 1|1]]

Therefore,
[MATH: P_{S}|= A(A^{T}A)^{− 1}A^{T}; = [1|1; 2|− 1; 1|1]([1|2|1; 1|− 1|1][1|1; 2|− 1; 1|1])^{− 1}[1|2|1; 1|− 1|1]; = [1|1; 2|− 1; 1|1][6|0; 0|3]^{− 1}[1|2|1; 1|− 1|1]; = [1|1; 2|− 1; 1|1] ⋅ (1)/(6)[1|0; 0|2] ⋅ [1|2|1; 1|− 1|1]; = (1)/(6)[1|1; 2|− 1; 1|1][1|2|1; 2|− 2|2]; = (1)/(2)[1|0|1; 0|2|0; 1|0|1].]

Item 8 — Tutorial: A Criterion of an Orthogonal Projection Matrix

Content:
A matrix [MATH: P] is an orthogonal projection matrix if and only if the following two conditions hold:

Content:
- [MATH: P^2 = P] (the matrix is idempotent), and
- [MATH: P^T = P] (the matrix is symmetric with respect to the main diagonal).

Content:
Let's check whether [MATH: [(1)/(2)|(1)/(2); (1)/(2)|(1)/(2)]] is an orthogonal projection matrix:

Content:
[MATH: A^{T}|= [(1)/(2)|(1)/(2); (1)/(2)|(1)/(2)]; = A.✓; A^{2}|= A ⋅ A; = [(1)/(2)|(1)/(2); (1)/(2)|(1)/(2)][(1)/(2)|(1)/(2); (1)/(2)|(1)/(2)]; = [(1)/(2)|(1)/(2); (1)/(2)|(1)/(2)]; = A.✓]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: A] is an orthogonal projection matrix.

---

Item 9 — Example: Identifying an Orthogonal Projection Matrix

Example Prompt:
Which of the following are orthogonal projection matrices?

[MATH: [2|1; 1|3]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that [MATH: Q] is an orthogonal projection matrix if and only if [MATH: Q^2=Q] and [MATH: Q^T=Q.]

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- [MATH: A] is not an orthogonal projection matrix. We have
[MATH: A^T = A]
but
[MATH: A^{2}|= A ⋅ A; = [2|1; 1|3][2|1; 1|3]; = [5|5; 5|10]; ≠ A.]
- [MATH: B] is not an orthogonal projection matrix. We have
[MATH: B^{T} ≠ B.]
- [MATH: C] is an orthogonal projection matrix. Indeed,
[MATH: C^T = C]
and
[MATH: C^{2}|= C ⋅ C; = [(4)/(5)|(2)/(5); (2)/(5)|(1)/(5)][(4)/(5)|(2)/(5); (2)/(5)|(1)/(5)]; = (1)/(5)[4|2; 2|1] ⋅ (1)/(5)[4|2; 2|1]; = (1)/(25)[4|2; 2|1][4|2; 2|1]; = (1)/(25)[20|10; 10|5]; = [(4)/(5)|(2)/(5); (2)/(5)|(1)/(5)]; = C.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: C] only."
